Hardtack is a type of extremely hard, dry, plain cracker or biscuit — so hard that if you try to bite into a dry piece without preparation, you could easily chip or break a tooth.

A piece of hardtack is flat, usually square or rectangular, roughly the size of a large cracker. It's pale cream or off-white in color, dense, and typically about half a centimeter thick. It usually has small holes punched through it to let steam escape during baking so it doesn't puff up.

Hardtack has an almost laughably simple recipe: just flour, water, and sometimes a pinch of salt. No butter, no eggs, no yeast, no sugar — nothing that would make bread soft, fluffy, or tasty. It's baked at low heat for a long time until every trace of moisture is driven out, leaving behind something closer to a flat rock than a biscuit.
Why it was made this way

The whole point of hardtack was survival, not enjoyment. Because it contains almost no moisture, bacteria and mold cannot grow in it. A well-made piece of hardtack can last for months, years, or even decades without spoiling — as long as it stays dry and free from insects. This made it one of the most practical foods imaginable in an era before refrigerators existed.

Three groups relied on hardtack most heavily throughout history:

Sailors on long ocean voyages. Fresh food would rot within days at sea, but hardtack could outlast a months-long journey. It was so common on ships that it earned the nickname "ship's biscuit" or "sea biscuit."

Soldiers during wars. During the American Civil War (1861–1865), hardtack was one of the primary foods issued to soldiers. It kept them fed on long marches and during weeks in camp far from any town or supply chain.

Explorers and pioneers crossing long stretches of wilderness. When you're traveling for weeks with no way to buy or cook fresh food, a bag of hardtack was the difference between eating and starving.

Nobody enjoyed eating hardtack dry — that would be like chewing gravel. People found clever ways to make it edible:

  • Soaking: Dunking a piece in water, coffee, soup, or any warm liquid for a few minutes would soften it enough to chew safely. This was the most common method.
  • Crumbling into a stew or soup: Broken-up pieces would slowly absorb liquid and become soft while adding bulk to a meal.
  • Frying in fat: Cooking it in a pan with grease or lard softened it and gave it a little flavor.

Here's the grimly fascinating part. During long storage — especially aboard ships — small beetles called weevils would burrow into hardtack and lay their eggs inside. Soldiers and sailors would tap their hardtack against a hard surface to knock the insects loose before eating, or eat it in the dark so they simply couldn't see what was crawling out of it.

This unpleasant reality gave hardtack a string of colorful nicknames:

  • "Worm castles"
  • "Tooth dullers"
  • "Molar breakers"
  • "Sheet iron crackers"

These nicknames weren't affectionate — they were complaints from people who had no other choice.

In the modern world, hardtack is mostly a historical curiosity. You can still buy it and some people make it at home, but it's no longer a food anyone depends on for survival. Survivalists and emergency-preparedness enthusiasts sometimes stock it precisely because of its legendary shelf life — a sealed container of hardtack could theoretically outlast you. It also shows up in historical reenactments and as a novelty food for people curious about what soldiers and sailors actually ate. As a daily staple, though, it has been entirely replaced by better options, which is something to be grateful for.

In short: hardtack is the no-frills, nearly indestructible emergency ration of the pre-refrigeration world — a food designed not to taste good, but simply to not go bad and keep people alive when nothing else was available.
